blocks.text: **The problem.** Two players take turns removing one number from **either end** of the array `nums`, adding it to their own score. Player 1 goes first, and both play as well as possible. Return `true` if Player 1 can **win or tie**.

blocks.alt: nums is 1, 5, 2. If Player 1 takes 1, Player 2 takes 5 and wins. If Player 1 takes 2, Player 2 takes 5 again. Either way Player 2 gets the 5, so Player 1 loses: the answer is false. The recursive question at each step: what's the best lead the player to move can get over the other on the numbers left?

elements.text: take from either end; each turn, the other player faces a smaller array
elements.originalText: take from either end; each turn, the other player faces a smaller array

blocks.code:
nums = [1, 5, 2]       ->  false   (Player 2 always gets the 5)
nums = [1, 5, 233, 7]  ->  true    (take 1; whatever Player 2 takes, 233 is reachable)
nums = [7]             ->  true

blocks.text: The idea: the best lead over the other player

Define `lead(l, r)` = the most the player **about to move** can end up ahead by, playing on `nums[l..r]`. If they take `nums[l]`, the opponent then moves on `nums[l+1..r]` and gets a lead of `lead(l + 1, r)` over **them** — so their lead is `nums[l] − lead(l + 1, r)`. Taking `nums[r]` works the same way. They pick the better: `lead(l, r) = max(nums[l] − lead(l+1, r), nums[r] − lead(l, r−1))`. With one number left, the lead is that number. Player 1 wins or ties when `lead(0, n−1) >= 0`. Thinking in **leads** means one function serves both players.

blocks.caption: The game tree: each node is a range still in play; its lead comes from its two children.

blocks.text: **Time O(2ⁿ), space O(n).** Every call branches twice. With n up to 20, that's about a million calls — acceptable here, but the same ranges are solved many times.
There are only n² different ranges `(l, r)`. Store each lead the first time — top-down dynamic programming.
**Time O(n²), space O(n²).** A bottom-up table filled by range length reaches the same time with O(n) memory — the interval pattern in the Dynamic Programming course.

blocks.alt: Plain recursion: O(2^n) time, O(n) space. Memoized ranges: O(n²) time, O(n²) space.

items: **A tie** — `[1, 1]`: equal scores count as a win for Player 1.
**Even length** — Player 1 can always win or tie (by taking all even-indexed or all odd-indexed numbers), a neat fact worth mentioning.
**Stone Game** — even length, so the answer is always true; the same recursion proves it.
**Stone Game II and III** — take one to three piles from the front: the same lead-based recursion with a different set of moves.
**Can I Win** — choose numbers from a pool: recursion with the used set as a bitmask.
